Question: I want to buy a used laptop for web development, but my budget is low. Which generation's laptop is preferable in 2024?
Answer: I’ll let you in on a secret that is the worst kept secret in the world. But this goes only for Windows machines. I get into Macs below. You can safely buy 8th and 9th gen laptop, CPU that starts with i5/i7 and the first number is like 8700 ort 9700, the last two numbers really don’t matter. Next comes a letter, usually U, H or Q, seldomly on laptops do you get K. I would try to go for i7 if possible, that is a sweat spot, i5 is noticeably slower and i9 is for cooking eggs, but if you need i9 go for it and i5 is just great if that is your budget, you are not loosing out here. U means the machine has decent battery life but it isn’t fast. If you work with some amount of data you could experience hiccups, like the machine stalls for a few milliseconds, enough to notice. Now, this does not have to happen but this is my experience. These machines are usually great for surfing, Office work and light games. Speaking only for myself, U means useless or Powerpoint computer But like MS Surface Pro/Book/Laptop will be great, amazing even. The K simply means the CPU can be overclocked, you might not want that in a laptop. H or Q usually means the machine is quite fast. Battery life isn’t great, 4 hours but you can squeeze out 6, all things depending. Often you have a discrete GPU like Nvidia or AMD. AMD CPU that is 4000/5000 models is pretty great, no matter which numbers follow, but 5600 is in my opinion above the line where things are awesome and below is not that bad, 3600 is probably just as good, little warmer perhaps. Having 6 cores is plentiful and some 2000/3000 line discrete GPU will take on whatever you want. Dell machines like XPS, Thinkpad machines that have names that start with T, P and W are great, Legion 5 Pro is great. Some examples, T490s, W530, P15v. T480 machines, and even T440 and between will work for most type of work but have slower storage disks. Asus and Acer make really great gaming machines. Now, ignore gaming, these machines are spectacular. They offer high refresh rate displays which are just something else, you might not notice just how amazing they are until you put another laptop next to it. The Helios, Predator and Nitro are all machines I have owned and really liked. These machines also tolerate being kicked, dropped and some hustling, there is a limit to everything. Alienware and Razor machines are absolutely fantastic but they usually cost a lot of money even if they are real old. The LCD colored keys on the computers, they don’t bother me and I am weird about things bothering me. I like it, plus it is great to use in a dark area AND bright. But Dell XPS, real Thinkpad machines (single letter with 2–3 numbers naming, no yoga or anything), Acer and Asus all offer (mostly all) the possibility of having 2 disks in them, either a combination of NvM and SSD or just 2 NvM. You can pour water on some of the Thinkpads and it will just run through the machine. Just make sure you have such a machine before you try it, coolest party trick ever. These machines are all 6–8 cores minimum and pack a power. I want to say all of them have amazing Linux support but I am sure people can find one that don’t. All of these have expandable memory and replaceable disks. Some of them have Thunderbolt or USBC. Just check what you need. But most of these actually have ETHERNET port which is very cool, HDMI, plenty of USB. Some could be expanded to 64GB memory and basically the biggest storage you can buy, 4TB/8TB is possible and not a limit of the computer but type of disc. Newer machines don’t offer plenty of ports, and most USBC dongles with display ports and so on suck badly and run HOT. As I write this in August 2024. I would buy a gaming machine that is even more than 2–3 years old. They might only cost like $500 or LESS. That is like getting a collection quality Mercedes Benz or rare Ferrari for $500. I have a rather new work laptop Thinkpad, P15v, (single letter real machine), but the fans are driving me nuts. Good machine but I would not buy one myself. I also have currently a thin Predator, it does have i7 10th gen, it has 32 GB memory, 1 TB disk NvM and space for another one. It has 300hz monitor, and let me tell you, this screen is so rock solid, it is like a high quality photo but it moves. Yes the fans come on and off but these are real fans, no high pitch noise which apparently only I and dogs hear. You can take this machine and beat someone with it and it won’t get damaged, I don’t speak from experience, just guessing. If you are buying a Mac. Don’t buy the Intel ones, even if you get it cheap and plan on using Windows or Linux, not unless it is like close to free, then all bets are off, decent machines, especially the 15 and 16 inch. I just can’t recommend it. You can buy any current Macbook out there and you are getting a great machine. Just one thing to note, don’t buy one with less than 16 GB memory and 500 GB storage. You are stuck with what you have. The 14/16 inch M1 Pro machines are going for just over $1000 or so, you can score a Mac Studio desktop for like $1300. These machines are amazing in every aspect, I own one. You will not hear a fan, it is so silent that it feels like it is turned off. The screen, sound in speakers are amazing. I basically say, go for 15″ Air if you can, it is really a sweet spot. The 14″ Pro is amazing but the 16 pro is just worth every penny and is more amazing, I can’t talk highly enough of it, buy me a beer and I will talk about it all day and night. I am a programmer. I work with a lot of data. My M1 Pro is 32GB and 1000GB storage, but I would be just as happy with 16/500. It is the best laptop on the market, hands down. I make crazy demands of my computers, much higher than my talent or needs require, but until very recently I have always owned brand new machines and sold them less than 1 years old, but today I am happy with 3–4 year old machines. I have owned the Predator for close to 3 years or going on 3 years, and bought it used. I have no plans on selling it. My Macbook pro M1 pro. I will probably own it for the next 3 years at least unless something changes dramatically. The 12th/13th/14th gen Intel laptops seem to have issues which cause random crashes, not everyone experiences it, but they all run very hot. The 11th gen is notorious for running dangerously hot. (The quote is just for attention). And they are expensive, Apple like expensive The 8/9/10 gen will serve you just great for years to come, and make you happy while you pay way less than 1/3 of the original price. Dell and Thinkpad often have an option of extended warranty, different from place to place. It is worth it. Basically if there is a repair shop in your city/town, they will fix it the next business day if you have one. Some models offer you to buy these within 3 years. I used to like HP machines but HP company is just not doing anything correct. I can not recommend any of their machines. But the 360 series and Spectre laptops sure look great. I would buy one that passes my tests and is working, cheap, but I would not expect great service from HP. In Iceland, the dealer for them is pretty good. But they usually only have the USA keyboard which I don’t like, no button between left shift and Z, and single height ENTER button. I am just not used to this and I don’t want it. That is me. Yes. Go and buy good cheap 4–5 generation old laptops. They are really amazing, that is the best ones from that era, the cheap garbage was garbage when it was new and is probably not available to buy because they have been thrown away already. Just test them, see the battery health, test all the keys, especially W A S D keys and space bar. All of the PC machines that are 4–5 gen (years old) are all serviceable, and you can get spare parts for them. PC laptops 1, Apple 0. TLDR; Given everything, it is quite safe to buy top end laptops from 4 years ago or 5 even. Just make sure you reset it to factory settings, you really don’t want anything from the old owner, they might have some scam software, even if it is full of games and crap. Working on a brand new laptop for $4000 or a 4–5 year old for $500. You will be hard pressed at finding any real speed difference in most things.

Question: Is asynchronous programming achieved by using multiple threads?
Answer: It could be. Like Elixir, DotNet, Go and such. They use all sorts of tricks that is outside of your controls. They might run on a different core but it is not guaranteed. Usually asynchronous is simply so called event loop. It is basically just an endless loop that has a list of tasks that need to be done. When you add a task by using async calls, you are added into the list. You get a promise back which keeps the status of your request. Behind the scenes there is a scheduler. It just goes over your task list and asks the promiser if they are done, if done it returns your data else it goes next in line and vice verse. If this is for example a restful API, each query it gets is also sent to the list or queue. The scheduler then simply gives each task a chance to run for a while, then it goes to the next one and that one runs for a while. So and so on. It usually runs on a single core, doing one thing at a time. This is also why if you ask for 5 things to be done, it finishes out of order. If you don’t call async, it will run everything in the sequence it got the work. But while it is running, everything else is blocked, meaning if you run a large task this way, write gigabytes to the storage. Nothing else runs until it is finished. That is called blocking call and should mostly not be used or called, but there are circumstances where it is needed. JavaScript and Node are guaranteed to run only on one core doing one thing at a time. You can use libraries which use more cores, but then you really should know what you are doing, locks, semaphores and all sorts of edge cases.
